titre: Vernon Sullivan, the Author Boris Vian Invented
accroche: In 1946, Boris Vian signs a noir novel with the name of an invented author; the scandal will lead him, four years later, to a conviction.
contenu_vulgarise:
## A Bet in a Movie Line

Summer 1946. The book is born of a bet made in a movie theater line. The publisher Jean d'Halluin is looking for a best seller to save his publishing house. His friend Boris Vian takes up the challenge: to write in two weeks a novel in the style of American noir novels. The story is set in the southern United States and tells of the revenge of a mixed-race man after the lynching of his brother. The Bibliothèque nationale de France (BnF) describes the book as erotic and provocative, and as a denunciation of the racism suffered by Black Americans.

## A Name That Is Not His

On November 21, 1946, *J'irai cracher sur vos tombes* (*I Spit on Your Graves*) appears under a pseudonym: Vernon Sullivan. The reception is at first very timid. Then scandal gets involved and the success becomes colossal: the book is the best seller of 1947. Signed with his real name, *L'Écume des jours* (*Froth on the Daydream*), published in March 1947, meets with no success in the lifetime of Vian, who died in June 1959: it would take until the late 1960s for the public to recognize it.

## The Mask Cracks

In April 1948, when Vian's real role in the book is widely suspected, an “original” version in English appears, *I Shall Spit on Your Graves* (The Vendôme Press). It is in reality the work of Vian, helped by Milton Rosenthal, an American friend who also contributed to *Les Temps modernes* (*Modern Times*): it serves to give a real existence to the fictional character of Vernon Sullivan. In August 1948, the Cartel d'action sociale et morale (Cartel for Social and Moral Action), led by Daniel Parker, files a new complaint. On November 24, 1948, Vian acknowledges being the author of the book and not its translator. On May 13, 1950, he is sentenced to a fine of 100,000 francs for “outrage aux bonnes mœurs” (offense against public decency). After several appeals, he is sentenced in October 1953 to fifteen days in prison, then amnestied.

## What the Pseudonym Did Not Protect

The two BnF pages retain only a single count, the offense against public decency. They detail neither the procedure nor the grounds of the judgment: so it cannot be said, from them, what the court made of the confession of 1948. What they establish is enough: the conviction targets Boris Vian. Simone de Beauvoir, in *La Force des choses* (*Force of Circumstance*), links this episode to the accusations against Jean-Paul Sartre: the books of both authors were held responsible for suicides, crimes, and murders.

The novel appeared under the name of Vernon Sullivan and became the best seller of 1947. That name nevertheless did not protect the man who held the pen: it is he, and not his character, whom the court convicted.

repere.texte: On May 13, 1950, Boris Vian is sentenced to a fine of 100,000 francs for “outrage aux bonnes mœurs” (offense against public decency) because of J'irai cracher sur vos tombes, published in 1946 under the name of Vernon Sullivan. In October 1953, after several appeals, he is sentenced to fifteen days in prison, then amnestied.
repere.source: Bibliothèque nationale de France, exhibition “Boris Vian”

carte.punch: Vernon Sullivan never existed: it was Boris Vian who was convicted.
carte.idee: In 1946, Boris Vian publishes a noir novel under the name of an invented author, Vernon Sullivan. The scandal makes it the best seller of 1947. On May 13, 1950, it is he, Vian, who is sentenced to a fine of 100,000 francs for “outrage aux bonnes mœurs” (offense against public decency).

quiz.question: On what grounds is Vian sentenced to a fine of 100,000 francs on May 13, 1950?
choix: For plagiarism of a real American novelist
For “outrage aux bonnes mœurs” (offense against public decency)
For defamation of the Cartel d'action sociale et morale
For usurping the name of a publisher
quiz.explication: The BnF retains only a single count: “outrage aux bonnes mœurs” (offense against public decency), for J'irai cracher sur vos tombes. Neither of the two pages mentions plagiarism, defamation, or usurpation, and they do not detail the procedure.

quiz_supplementaire.question: In April 1948, how does Vian try to give reality to the fictional character of Vernon Sullivan?
choix: By publishing a fake biography in the New York press
By signing a contract with a real American literary agent
By writing, with the American Milton Rosenthal, a fake “original” English version of the novel
By having the book illustrated by an American artist
quiz_supplementaire.explication: While his role is already widely suspected, Vian has an “original” English version of the novel published with Milton Rosenthal, an American friend and contributor to Les Temps modernes, to give reality to the character of Vernon Sullivan.

quiz_supplementaire.question: What happens to Boris Vian after the legal appeals that follow the 1950 conviction?
choix: He is acquitted on appeal and the book can again be sold without restriction
He is expelled from the Cartel d'action sociale et morale for defamation
The court doubles the amount of the initial fine, to 200,000 francs
In October 1953, he is sentenced to fifteen days in prison, immediately amnestied
quiz_supplementaire.explication: After several appeals, Vian is sentenced in October 1953 to fifteen days in prison, immediately amnestied. The BnF pages mention neither an acquittal nor a doubling of the fine.
